| **Privilege level**             | Low / unprivileged                               | Highest / fully privileged                         |
| **Access to hardware**      | Almost none directly                             | Full & direct access (ports, MMU, interrupts…)     |
| **Memory access**           | Only own process's virtual address space         | Entire physical memory + all virtual spaces        |
| **Allowed instructions**      | Normal instructions + system calls               | All instructions (including privileged ones: HLT, IN/OUT, LGDT, MOV to CR*, etc.) |
| **What runs here**            | Your apps (Chrome, VS Code, games, etc.)         | OS kernel, drivers, schedulers, file systems, memory manager… |
| **Crash impact**                | Usually just the process dies (segfault, etc.)   | Usually crashes/panics the whole system (BSOD, kernel oops, panic) |
| **Purpose**                     | Run untrusted / buggy code safely                | Manage hardware and enforce rules on user code     |
| **Typical address space part**  | Lower addresses (user space)                     | Upper addresses (kernel space) — often mapped everywhere |
The CPU starts in kernel mode during boot.

- Or hardware **interrupt** / **exception** / **trap** (page fault, timer tick, disk I/O complete…)

Without the file abstraction, programming would be dramatically harder: every program would need to know about disk geometry, manage free space itself, invent its own naming scheme, handle concurrency, etc.

The file (together with the directory tree) is the OS's gift that lets us pretend persistent storage is just a big, named, random-access array of bytes that multiple programs can use safely at the same time.

| Order | Topic                          | Why after OS? / What it builds on                              | Typical difficulty | Usefulness in 2026 job market |

| 1     | **Computer Networks**                                          | OS already introduced sockets + basic I/O → now understand the network stack below | Medium             | Extremely high                |

| 2     | **Databases / Database Systems**                            | Heavy use of OS concepts (files, concurrency, caching, crash recovery)                      | Medium–Hard        | Very high                     |

| 3     | **Distributed Systems**                                          | OS concepts scaled to many machines (concurrency ×1000, partial failure, clocks)        | Hard               | High (cloud, backend)         |

| 4     | **Compilers / Programming Language Implementation** | Deepens understanding of abstraction layers (OS is one; now see how languages work) | Hard               | Medium–High (if → tools/lang) |

| 5     | **Computer Security / Cybersecurity**                       | OS protection mechanisms are the foundation; now attacks & defenses                     | Medium–Hard        | Very high                     |

| 6     | **Cloud Computing & Virtualization** (optional early)     | Directly extends OS virtualization, containers (Docker), Kubernetes                           | Medium             | Very high                     |

| 7     | **Advanced OS topics**                                           | Multicore scheduling, real-time, file system internals, kernel dev                              | Hard               | Medium (systems jobs)         |

| 8     | **System Programming** / **Performance Engineering** | Writing fast, reliable low-level code using OS facilities                                           | Hard               | High (backend/infra)          |

| 9     | **Machine Learning Systems** / **ML Infrastructure**   | How training & serving works at scale (very OS/dist-sys heavy now)                        | Hard               | Extremely high if ML path     |

| 10    | **Embedded Systems / Real-Time OS**                       | OS concepts under extreme constraints (no MMU, tiny RAM, deadlines)                    | Hard               | Medium–High (IoT, automotive) |

The OS represents each process with a PCB (container with the information about the process), that has:
— address of the next instruction to execute
— page tables, segment info, base/limit registers
— priority, time slice, CPU affinity, queue links, nice value
— open files, handles, devices, pending I/O, file descriptors
— CPU time used, start time, resource usage, quotas
